channel.title: EmberSeed AI News
channel.description: The AI news worth knowing, in plain English. Summarised by AI, read by Andrew.

item.title: SAP reportedly plans at least 10,000 job cuts
item.description: German software firm SAP is reportedly preparing to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it reshapes its business for AI, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. SAP told CNBC that roles will change over time but that no decisions have been made on further measures. The company, which employs more than 110,000 people, cut about 10,000 positions in a 2024 reorganisation, mostly through voluntary departures and retraining. Why it matters: If your business relies on SAP software, the reported cuts are unconfirmed, so ask your vendor contact how support and service may change. Source: CNBC Technology.

item.title: Nvidia pauses server shipments to four Southeast Asian nations
item.description: Nvidia has asked manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and Financial Times. The Journal says the pause has no set end date while Nvidia checks whether regional partners meet US export rules. The move follows a US crackdown on Chinese firms renting Nvidia-powered computing remotely from data centres in those countries. Data centres already supplying large amounts of computing power to China-based companies have 90 days from 19 November to obtain a US licence, and banks have reportedly halted about US$500 million in loans to one provider, Aolani. Why it matters: If you use cloud servers based in Southeast Asia, ask your provider whether the new US licence rules affect your service. Reporters quote an executive saying there is no clear guidance yet. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Talkie blocks Australian web users after Apple removal
item.description: Talkie, a popular AI companion app, now blocks web visitors in Australia and the UK. The move follows Apple's global removal of the app after a joint ABC and Bureau of Investigative Journalism investigation into inappropriate chats with children. The investigation also reported evidence that parent company MiniMax trained its models on chats users were told were private. Australia's eSafety Commissioner is investigating the app, and MiniMax did not respond to questions about the blocking. Why it matters: If your business runs a chatbot or collects customer chat data, check your privacy wording. The Children's Online Privacy Code starts 10 December, but the report doesn't say which businesses it covers. Source: ABC News.

item.title: Sydney start-up Ante plans zero-human software company
item.description: Sydney entrepreneur Lambros Photios has launched Ante, which he says will soon be Australia's first "zero-human company". His team built the product in about 10 days by cloning existing software, aiming to replace Atlassian's Confluence. Photios wants Ante running with no daily human input by March. University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson says a company without human oversight would be illegal and could be prosecuted. Why it matters: If you pay for subscription software, AI can now copy some tools quickly, so review renewals. Australian companies still need a human director who is liable when things go wrong. Source: ABC News.

item.title: TrueLayer's AI agent makes first cardless UK pizza purchase
item.description: TrueLayer says an AI agent has made the first UK cardless purchase, ordering nine mini pizzas from Papa John's. The order ran in the Financial Conduct Authority's regulated sandbox, using Lloyds Bank, and used no account numbers or passwords. The agent worked under a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month. TrueLayer chief executive Francesco Simoneschi calls the test a first step toward public use. Why it matters: Not yet announced for Australia. If you sell online, ask your payment provider whether it plans to support AI-agent purchases, and how refunds would work. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: OpenAI fixes billing bug, tightening GPT-6.2 usage limits
item.description: A billing bug gave most users the wrong discounts on GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, according to OpenAI Codex engineer Thibault Sottiaux. Now that it's fixed, usage limits run out 40 percent faster on Astra and 25 percent faster on Sol than last week. OpenAI won't charge retroactively for the difference. Go, Plus, Pro and Business subscribers get an extra saved reset, and Business users get free Fast Mode access until the end of the year. Why it matters: If your team uses GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol on a paid plan, expect usage limits to run out sooner than last week. Plan heavy work around that, and use the extra saved reset. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Z.AI and Moonshot delay flagship models as US curbs bite
item.description: Chinese AI firms Z.AI and Moonshot AI are delaying their next flagship models as US restrictions tighten. Reuters, citing sources, says Z.AI's GLM-5.5, planned for November, will likely slip into the first quarter of 2027. InnovationAus reports that Moonshot's development cycle could double from six months to a year or longer without access to overseas computing power. OpenAI and Anthropic have blocked data scraping for distillation, so Moonshot is reportedly turning to the latest Google and Meta models for training. Why it matters: If your business uses Chinese AI models, expect slower upgrades. Check your provider's roadmap before committing to a long-term contract. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Microsoft maps how state hackers use the ARTEX AI tool
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence says state-backed groups from China and North Korea have built the ARTEX AI attack tool into their operations. Released in July 2026, the penetration-testing framework uses specialised AI agents to automate attacks from reconnaissance through to data theft. In one case, an agent took five minutes to pull data from Azure Key Vault, and a Storm-0940 campaign logged more than 151,000 failed logins. Microsoft recommends decoy systems, slow-response traps and strict access controls, and says its own tests sharply cut successful attack traffic. Why it matters: If your business runs cloud accounts or online logins, ask your IT provider about access controls and rate limits, which Microsoft recommends against automated attacks. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: 42 US state attorneys general oppose Character.AI chat auction
item.description: A bipartisan group of 42 US state attorneys general wants a bankruptcy court to block Character.AI's 1 December auction of users' private chats. The AGs say the data covers more than 21 million US accounts, over 2.1 million of them registered to minors. Character.AI says its privacy policy still protects users, but the AGs argue that buyers would not have to honour it. If this raises concerns for you, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. Why it matters: If your business runs a chatbot that stores customer conversations, check what your privacy promises would mean if the provider went bankrupt and sold its data. Source: The Verge.

item.title: 76% of Australians have mistaken AI content for real
item.description: Researchers at the University of Canberra report that 76% of Australians have recently believed AI-generated content was real, only to learn later that it wasn't. Their survey of 2,000 adults ran in August and September 2026. Trust is low: 34% said they trust ChatGPT, 24% trust Microsoft Copilot, 24% trust Google Gemini and 17% trust Claude. The authors, writing in The Conversation, argue that platforms need clearer AI labels and that adults need media and AI literacy training. Why it matters: If your business posts images, video or written content online, customers may not be able to tell whether it was made with AI. Label AI-made material and check facts before you publish. Source: The Conversation.

item.title: Nine pilots licensed AI access to its journalism
item.description: Nine is piloting a way for corporate subscribers to query its papers inside their AI tools. The pilot covers the AFR, SMH, The Age, Brisbane Times and WAtoday, linked through MCP, an open connection standard. Nine says it is co-designing the service with business clients before a commercial rollout through 2027. It has not disclosed which AI platforms are supported, what licensees will pay, or whether they receive full articles. Why it matters: If your business holds a corporate subscription to Nine's papers, this could reach your AI tools as the rollout runs through 2027. Nine hasn't said what licensees will pay or whether full articles are included, so check the terms before you budget. Source: iTnews.

item.title: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
item.description: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a five-year ban on making, distributing and selling AI chatbot toys, such as talking stuffed animals and dolls. The state is the second after California to ban them. The law takes effect 90 days after signing, and violators face civil penalties of up to US$15,000 per day for each violation, enforced by the attorney general. A Common Sense Media study this week found about a quarter of American parents with children under eight own or are considering an AI toy. Why it matters: If you stock or sell AI toys into New York, the ban will apply to those sales once it takes effect. The sources don't mention any Australian rules on these toys. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: OpenAI merges ChatGPT Chat and Work usage limits
item.description: OpenAI has begun rolling out a merged Chat and Work experience to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault Sottiaux said on X. Chat and Work will share one usage meter, though conversations on the Instant model stay unlimited and don't count toward it. OpenAI says most users won't face more frequent resets, but a small fraction of heavy users may hit their limits sooner. A wider rollout is planned for December, and no Australian timing has been announced. Why it matters: If your team leans heavily on ChatGPT, watch your usage after the December rollout, as the heaviest users may hit limits sooner. Chats on the Instant model won't count toward the shared allowance. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Nothing's Ear (note) earbuds turn talks into notes
item.description: Nothing has given its Ear (note) AI earbuds a detailed look ahead of their 8 December release. The buds can record calls, while the charging case records, transcribes and summarises conversations. Bloomberg reports the buds will connect to a companion app that manages recordings, transcripts and AI summaries. Pricing, specifications and Australian availability have not yet been announced. Why it matters: If your team takes client calls, set a recording and consent policy before staff start using these. Pricing is not yet announced, so hold off budgeting for them. Source: The Verge.

item.title: EA brings AI-recreated John Motson voice to FC 27
item.description: EA Sports is adding an AI-recreated voice of late commentator John Motson to FC 27 on 26 November. EA says Motson's widow and son approved it, and the family was paid, though it won't say how much. Motson died in February 2023, and the voice draws on recordings from his FIFA years. Peter Caulfield of Save Our Voices Now raises concerns that Motson never consented himself, while EA says it won't replace commentators. Why it matters: If you use a real person's voice or likeness in ads, get explicit written consent that covers AI use. Here, one campaigner argues family approval wasn't enough. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: FCC clears SpaceX's Starmind AI satellite constellation
item.description: US regulator the FCC has approved SpaceX's plan for up to 1 million AI satellites, called Starmind. SpaceX says the satellites would use solar power and send data to Earth by laser through its Starlink network. The licence requires at least one satellite deployed by November 2033 and the full fleet by 2040. The FCC deferred SpaceX's request to move older satellites to "graveyard" orbits, saying it lacked sufficient detail. Amazon calls the plan a "lofty ambition", and US astronomers warn it would hurt night-sky viewing. Why it matters: Don't plan around this yet. The licence requires the first satellite by 2033, though SpaceX says it wants to launch next year, and the BBC reports it is unclear whether all one million will launch. Your AI costs still depend on today's cloud options. Source: The Verge.

item.title: WA suspends Deloitte for three months over AI errors
item.description: The WA government has suspended Deloitte from most government work for up to three months over an AI-riddled report. The report analysed a proposed merger of Curtin, Murdoch and the University of Western Australia. The government has ordered Deloitte to refund its A$166,000 fee, which Tertiary Education Minister Tony Buti says is still unpaid. Deloitte calls the errors "minor" and says they don't affect the findings. Why it matters: If you hire consultants to write reports, ask how AI is used and who checks the output. Agree refund terms in writing before you sign. Source: ABC News.

item.title: Tidal bans fully AI-generated music from 9 December
item.description: Streaming service Tidal will remove fully AI-generated music from 9 December, deleting existing tracks as well. Music lead Robert Andersen says 43% of tracks uploaded in the past 90 days were AI-generated, and earlier labelling was not enough. Tidal estimates it will delete around 29 million songs and reject 80,000 to 85,000 tracks a day. Music made with AI assistance is still allowed, as long as AI isn't the sole output. Why it matters: If you license music for your business or distribute tracks for clients, check any AI-made audio. From 9 December, Tidal will reject fully AI-generated songs, though AI-assisted work is still accepted. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Anthropic study finds AI adoption stalls on internal friction
item.description: Anthropic's "Working with AI" report finds that most roadblocks to workplace AI sit inside companies, not in the software. Researchers conducted 66 in-person interviews at 58 US companies, all Anthropic customers, so the sample isn't representative. Respondents say 55 percent of nearly 300 live AI projects raised output or quality, but 19 percent delivered no business value. The most common obstacle was the volume of AI output staff still need to check. Why it matters: If you roll out AI in your business, budget for staff checking its output before you count the time savings. In this study, that checking was the top snag. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Amazon reportedly in talks to let Meta's Muse shop
item.description: Amazon and Meta are reportedly in talks that could let Meta's Muse AI agent shop on Amazon's store. Muse users began hitting checkout errors on Amazon about two months ago. Fortune's sources say Amazon is concerned about advertising revenue, search quality and its relationship with customers. Any deal would need both companies' CEOs to approve it, and neither company has responded to requests for comment. Why it matters: If you sell on Amazon, nothing is agreed yet, but a deal could change how AI shopping agents find and buy your products. Keep your listings accurate and up to date. Source: The Verge.

item.title: University of Sydney makes honours students defend theses orally
item.description: All students in the University of Sydney's one-year honours program must now sit an oral assessment, as AI makes written theses an unreliable measure. Formats differ by faculty: one student's pass-or-fail conversation counts for nothing towards his grade, while another's hour-long interview made up half of hers. The university says it can't reliably restrict AI use in honours theses and will take feedback into its 2027 planning. One student calls the demand insulting. Why it matters: If you hire honours graduates, expect some to have defended their theses aloud, as Sydney, Melbourne, Monash and Australian Catholic University move this way. Ask candidates to walk you through their research. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: Amazon buys Decart to sharpen its Trainium chips
item.description: Amazon is acquiring AI startup Decart's technology and team in a deal reported at US$7.5 billion. The core asset is Decart Optimization Stack, software that helps AI models run better on non-Nvidia chips. Amazon says it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimise its Trainium chips, and TechCrunch says the deal looks aimed at speeding that up. Amazon is not taking on Decart's world-model work, while Anthropic reportedly tried to buy the startup for a similar price. Why it matters: If your business runs on AWS, this could eventually mean more options for Trainium-based computing. No timeline has been given, so there is nothing to act on yet. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Lenders grow pickier as Big Tech borrows for AI
item.description: Big Tech firms may find it harder to borrow for AI as bond investors become choosier. PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to sell about US$250 billion of bonds this year. Man Group analysis says Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are on track to spend more on capital projects than they generate in cash in both 2026 and 2027. L&G's Matthew Rees says some BBB-rated names, including Oracle, trade more like single B debt. Why it matters: If you pay for cloud or AI tools from big providers, their heavy spending and borrowing is worth watching. Check contract terms before committing to multi-year deals. Source: CNBC Technology.

item.title: Federal AI committee urges copyright payments for creators
item.description: A parliamentary committee on AI tabled its report on 24 November with 46 recommendations, including a mechanism to help Australian creators get paid by AI firms. The majority view also calls for transparency about how Australian content is used. Aria and Apra Amcos dispute that copyright changes are needed, and more than 7,000 artists have signed a pledge against weakening the law. Senator David Pocock, who dissented, wants a three-year moratorium on copyright changes. Why it matters: If your business relies on original content, such as photos, copy or music, watch the copyright debate. The committee's findings aren't government policy yet, and draft AI laws are expected early next year. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: Iran-linked fake reporter used ChatGPT to target Australia
item.description: OpenAI says it disrupted an Iran-based influence operation that used ChatGPT to create seven fake Western journalists. The ABC reports that one persona, Alice Johnson, published at least two articles and several posts about Australia, since removed. One article ran on Middle East Monitor in March, a site Semrush estimates had about 22,000 Australian visits in October. Foreign Minister Penny Wong will raise the case in federal parliament, and OpenAI has yet to respond to the ABC's request for comment. Why it matters: If your team relies on online news or social media for industry updates, check who wrote a story and where it came from before you act on it or repost it. Source: ABC News.

item.title: OpenAI brings GPT-6.2 Sol chat upgrade to paid plans
item.description: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide to paid ChatGPT users on Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise plans. OpenAI says it handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6. In its internal tests, image understanding rose from 47.4 to 71.7 per cent. Its system card puts safety-policy compliance in difficult conversations at 91 to 94 per cent, up from 77 to 80. Why it matters: If your team uses ChatGPT chat, check who has access: Enterprise admins decide whether users get GPT-6.2. The reported gains apply only to chat, not Work or Codex. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Meta brings its Muse AI agent to the UK
item.description: Meta has launched Muse, its personal AI agent, in the UK from 24 November for adults aged 18 and over. Meta says Muse can book travel and check out purchases, but it asks for approval before sending emails or buying anything. It runs on iOS, Android, the web at muse.ai and WhatsApp, and is free for most uses, with subscription plans for heavier use. According to The Guardian, UK regulators say they are keeping a close eye on the launch over privacy and consumer protection. An Australian launch is not yet announced. Why it matters: If you use Muse for email or shopping, decide which accounts it can reach. You approve every purchase, but you choose which other tasks it can carry out without asking. Source: Meta Newsroom.

item.title: CrowdStrike buys Zscaler in US$43.9 billion share deal
item.description: CrowdStrike will buy fellow security firm Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth US$43.9 billion. Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they hold. CEO George Kurtz calls the pairing a "winning combination" that adds network security to its platform. Investors are weighing dilution, and IG Group analyst Axel Rudolph says antitrust scrutiny is possible but premature to assume a block. Why it matters: If you buy security tools from CrowdStrike or Zscaler, ask your provider how the deal could affect pricing and support. The deal is not expected to close until the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. Source: CNBC Technology.

item.title: Google Search's AI Mode gets Wallet and Drive access
item.description: Google is extending Personal Intelligence, its feature that draws on users' own apps, to AI Mode in Search. Google Wallet is rolling out from today, with Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks. Google says AI Mode can only read Wallet accounts, not move or manage money. Connecting apps is optional, and the feature already works with Gmail, Calendar and Photos. Australian availability has not yet been announced. Why it matters: If your team uses Google Search for work, decide whether business documents or accounts should be connected. Connections are optional and can be switched off at any time. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: AWS-backed survey finds AI gains hard to measure across Asia
item.description: Some 58% of Asia-Pacific businesses using AI say their investments have already surpassed their initial costs. Yet only 12% are very confident they can accurately measure that return on investment. The research, by Strand Partners for Amazon Web Services, surveyed 9,750 business leaders in 10 Asia-Pacific markets. Australia had the region's highest adoption rate at 61%, while 48% of respondents cite a shortage of AI and digital skills as a barrier. Why it matters: If you can't yet measure what AI returns, set a baseline now, such as hours per task, before spending more. Source: CNBC Technology.

item.title: Safety groups ask Amazon and eBay to pause AI toys
item.description: More than 150 child safety groups and experts have urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys this Christmas until they are proved safe, and to offer refunds to buyers. Alliance 4 Children found one plush bunny, listed for ages three and up and connected to ChatGPT, suggested a child could consent to being touched for pleasure. US PIRG's tests of seven AI toys found most too faulty for sale, with privacy problems. Amazon says it has removed the named products while it reviews the claims; eBay says it continually evaluates its policies. Why it matters: If you buy AI toys for children, check the age rating and what data they collect, as testers found gaps in both. If you sell toys on Amazon or eBay, AI toy listings are now under close scrutiny. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after 11 days
item.description: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, effective immediately, 11 days after he resigned on 12 November. The board says it consulted senior US government officials before deciding Huang poses no national security risk. Nvidia shares opened about 30% higher on Monday, after the board said on 17 November it did not intend to bring him back. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, had been interim CEO. Why it matters: If your business relies on AI services, many run on Nvidia's chips, so a leadership change at the top can ripple outwards. Note which tools you depend on and whether you have a backup option. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok deepfakes
item.description: Oregon and Virginia have sued SpaceX in state courts, alleging it misled users about Grok's safety. The states allege SpaceX misrepresented its efforts against child sexual abuse material and nonconsensual intimate images. Virginia says its investigators found Grok's image safeguards "inconsistent and ineffective". The states seek civil penalties, and SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Why it matters: If you use AI image tools for marketing, don't take a vendor's safety claims on trust. Ask what it blocks and how it handles reports of abuse. Source: Wired.

item.title: Walmart opens its website to Meta's Muse agent
item.description: Walmart is letting Meta's Muse AI agent buy products on its website on a customer's behalf. Muse shopping goes live on 24 November, after a 24-hour delay, according to Walmart. Muse shops through an Agent Profile inside the customer's Walmart account, where users can set spending limits, approve purchases and review Muse's purchase history. Walmart says more AI agents and apps are on the way, while Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from their platforms. No Australian availability has been announced. Why it matters: If your team buys from Walmart, Muse can build a basket, but you set the spending limit and approve purchases. Source: The Verge.

item.title: OpenAI's Pachocki proposes shared AI limits tied to perplexity
item.description: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has proposed that AI developers agree on common limits, measured by a metric called perplexity. Perplexity scores how well a model predicts the next token, the chunks of text AI firms bill by; lower is better. In a blog post on 22 November, Pachocki says the score has stayed informative as task-based tests have aged quickly. He suggests companies would commit not to go past a set threshold until they can reliably monitor AI behaviour. Sam Altman called the post the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while. Why it matters: This is a proposal, not a rule, and no limits have been agreed, so nothing changes for your AI tools yet. If your business relies on a particular AI vendor, watch whether it signs up to shared limits. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Lottery Corporation stages small Genesys pilot for contact centre
item.description: The Lottery Corporation is transforming its contact centre through a smaller, staged pilot that won Board approval. The initial Genesys investment is $135,000, with partner QPC assisting, after earlier multi-million-dollar proposals failed to win Board support. General manager Tammy Hall told the Genesys Xperience APAC summit that the organisation is using about 20 percent of the platform's capability so far. The centre's roughly 140 staff handle calls on prize payments, complaints and responsible play, the industry term for gambling assistance. Why it matters: If you're pitching a big tech upgrade, a small staged pilot with a clear return may get the nod where a large plan stalls. Ask vendors to explain AI charges billed per token, the text chunks AI firms count. Source: iTnews.

item.title: Sierra doubles valuation to $30B in six months
item.description: Sierra, the customer experience company co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, has raised US$1.75 billion at a US$30 billion valuation. The Series F round, led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, comes six months after a round that valued the company at US$15 billion. Sierra says it serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies and that its outcome-based pricing helped double run-rate revenue to US$400 million within five months. Why it matters: If you're buying AI for customer service, ask vendors how they charge. Sierra says its outcome-based pricing helped double revenue, so per-result models are worth comparing. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Nicalis pulls AI music from Binding of Isaac update
item.description: Nicalis has removed AI-generated music from The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus after players raised concerns. According to The Verge, a Reddit user found tracks with Suno metadata in a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. Creator Edmund McMillen apologised on X, saying he "had no idea" generative AI was used. Steam reviews remain "overwhelmingly negative" despite the update. Why it matters: If you publish content made with AI, check where each file came from before it goes live. Valve requires Steam developers to disclose generative AI use, and this update drew a review backlash. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Lean community verifies Alpöge's Riemann hypothesis proof
item.description: The Lean and Mathlib communities say Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. Alpöge, described by The Guardian as an Anthropic mathematician, posted the proof on 20 November. The proof runs to 17 million lines of Lean, a language that checks each logical step. Alpöge credits Claude with help over about six weeks, while The Conversation calls it a proof no human can read. Why it matters: If AI produces work for your business, ask how it can be checked. Here, checking software backed the proof, but The Conversation says no human can read it. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash
item.description: Etsy has defended a new Terms of Use clause that lets it and third-party partners use seller content to train AI. Some sellers have left the platform over the change, which takes effect on 16 December, according to Engadget and The New York Times. Etsy's VP of operations, James Ossman, says the company does not use content to train models that copy original work or replace creativity. He says Etsy already uses seller content for translations, marketing and shop-performance tools, and bars AI crawlers from scraping listings. Why it matters: If you sell on Etsy, read the terms change before 16 December. It lets Etsy and partners use your listings to train AI, though Etsy says it won't copy your work. Source: Engadget.

item.title: Trump threatens US firms with tax over overseas data centres
item.description: US President Donald Trump said on Friday, 20 November, that American companies will not be allowed to build AI data centres overseas, and any that do could face a "tremendous tax". Speaking after a summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, he offered few details and said his own staff had not heard the idea before. The BBC reports it remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced. It also notes that Meta and Google have already agreed to build overseas data centres. Why it matters: This is a proposal with few details, not a rule yet. If your business uses AI tools run by US cloud providers, it's worth watching how this develops. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Signal blocks screenshots to keep AI agents out
item.description: Signal is restricting screenshots in its app on Android and iOS 27 to stop AI agents reading private messages. Its president, Meredith Whittaker, says built-in assistants such as Siri and Gemini can read on-screen content and undermine the app's privacy guarantees. Users can switch screenshots back on in settings, but Signal warns that could expose their chats to AI agents. Whittaker calls the fix incomplete, as agents can still reach app data through the device file system, and urges Apple, Google and Microsoft to offer developer tools. Why it matters: If your team shares sensitive details on Signal, expect screenshots to be blocked on phones. Signal says AI assistants may still reach messages another way, so don't treat the app as fully protected. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Apple hires engineers for its own AI agent
item.description: Apple is building its own AI agent, according to a job listing Bloomberg spotted before it was removed. The role seeks an engineer to lead an assistant that browses the web, works across apps, writes code and calls services. Bloomberg says the agent is at an early stage and could arrive as early as late next year, with no Australian timing announced. Separately, Bloomberg reports that macOS 27.3 now requires 14 steps, not four, for third-party agents such as ChatGPT to control Macs; Apple says the change protects users. Why it matters: If your team uses ChatGPT on Macs, expect extra setup steps before it can control the screen. Apple's own agent is still early, so don't build plans around it yet. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Anthropic shares slip back near IPO price in sell-off
item.description: Anthropic's shares closed down 8.5% on Friday 20 November, giving back half of Thursday's gains after its Nasdaq debut. The fall came during a wider tech sell-off that pushed the S&P 500 and Dow Jones into correction territory, according to the BBC. The stock dipped to about US$85 at one point, close to its US$83 listing price. CNBC reports the IPO raised a record US$93.5 billion. Why it matters: If you own shares or tech-heavy super funds, expect sharper daily swings while investors reassess AI spending. Source: BBC Technology.

item.title: BBC's TV test finds AI Black Friday advice mixed
item.description: The BBC tested four free AI assistants by asking each to find a 55-inch TV deal ahead of Black Friday. ChatGPT and Claude recommended TVs that were unavailable or led to dead pages, while Alexa's prices were accurate but it only searches Amazon's own store. Gemini gave a comparison table with no store links. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November, and its Australian availability is not yet announced. Why it matters: If you use a chatbot to hunt for sales, check each price, stock level and link on the seller's site before you buy. Wrong prices can waste time and money, and the BBC's test was not a formal study. Source: BBC Technology.

item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims Riemann hypothesis proof with Claude
item.description: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, a problem first proposed in 1859, working with Claude. The Verge reports the claim is unverified and that Anthropic has not commented. TechCrunch reports several mathematicians in an online chat say they have compiled his proof in Lean, a language for checking proofs, but understanding it will take time. The Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers a US$1 million prize per Millennium Prize problem, has not yet accepted it, and its rules require at least two years of scrutiny. Why it matters: If your business uses AI for complex technical work, big claims can take months or years to verify. Check important AI-generated results independently before you act on them. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Thinking Machines launches open Inkling 2 Mini for laptops
item.description: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open model that reasons longer without generating more text. It handles text and images and is licensed under Apache 2.0, with weights available on Hugging Face. On agentic coding tests, where AI carries out multi-step programming jobs, it reportedly leads open models under 100 billion parameters. Artificial Analysis rates it level with Qwen3.8 27B on its Intelligence Index, at roughly six times lower cost. Why it matters: If you handle sensitive customer records, a model that runs on a Mac with at least 32 GB of memory could keep that data on your own machine. Trial it on your own work before trusting published scores. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Google's Gemini on Mac gains computer use
item.description: Google has added computer use to its Gemini app for macOS, so the AI can run multi-step tasks across files, apps and websites. Users pick which apps Gemini may access, and can follow its progress in a live preview within the chat. They can pause, stop or approve actions as the AI works. The feature is rolling out in English to US users, and requires a Google AI Plus, Pro or Ultra subscription. Why it matters: If you're in Australia, this isn't available yet, and Google hasn't said when it will expand. When it does, review which folders and apps you grant access to before approving any actions. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Auto & General pilots AI agents for routine service queries
item.description: Insurer Auto & General is starting a pilot of Genesys' Agentic Virtual Agent (AVA) in one low-risk, high-volume part of its customer service. Head of unified communications Kelly Lyons told the Genesys Xperience APAC summit the insurer hopes the project becomes a blueprint for repeated customer journeys. The business already uses Genesys' Cloud Agent Copilot to summarise conversations, producing about 133,000 summaries a month in its service business. Why it matters: If your inbox is full of simple, repeat questions, that's a sensible place to start with AI. Pick one well-understood workflow, prove it works, then expand. Source: iTnews.

item.title: Anthropic lists on Nasdaq, closes first day 17% higher
item.description: Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, has begun trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Shares opened at US$111.50, above the US$83 IPO price, and closed near US$97, about 17% higher, according to The Guardian. TechCrunch reports the offering will raise over US$81 billion, while the wider market fell sharply that day. Its S-1 filing shows a US$80.7 billion first-half net loss, mostly from an accounting charge, against US$16.3 billion in revenue. Why it matters: If your business relies on Claude, nothing changes for your plan today. Anthropic's filing says founders, not shareholders, keep control, but watch for any pricing or terms notices. Source: The Verge.

item.title: US firms use more AI as token prices fall
item.description: US companies are using AI more than ever and paying less for it, according to the Ramp AI Index. Tokens, the units AI firms bill by, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, while volume hit a record high. Token spending fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier, according to Ramp, which tracks more than 85,000 US companies. OpenRouter's separate data shows a similar pattern, though neither source represents the whole market. Why it matters: If your business pays for AI by usage, per-token prices are falling, so check current rates before you renew. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: OpenAI tests Dots agents with some ChatGPT Plus users
item.description: OpenAI is testing Dots, its proactive AI agents, with a small group of ChatGPT Plus users. Dots first launched on Pro and higher plans, and can interact with over 4,000 apps while working on tasks in the background. Engadget reports that all ChatGPT Business Standard users are rolling out Dots from 20 November. Australian availability has not yet been announced, and OpenAI hasn't said whether the Plus access will be permanent. Why it matters: If your team is on ChatGPT Business Standard, Dots can now act in your apps and on your PC, so decide what access they get. Plus access may be temporary, so don't build workflows around it yet. Source: Engadget.

item.title: Meta's Muse agent reportedly mixing up users' private data
item.description: Meta employees have raised concerns that its AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations across accounts and exposing private user data, according to a Reuters report covered by TechCrunch. Staff described receiving childcare requests, product orders and bank balances that belonged to other people. One employee said Muse prompted her to reply to a Signal message from her sister, and that she had never granted it access to other apps. Meta says employee testing is core to development and that staff use versions of Muse different from the public one. Muse launched in September and has more than 10 million downloads. Why it matters: If you let staff connect AI agents to email, banking or messaging apps, check what each one can see and switch off access you don't need. The report doesn't say whether Muse is available in Australia. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Google adds recent AI chat sidebar to desktop homepage
item.description: Google has added a collapsible sidebar to AI Mode on its desktop homepage that lists recent searches. Google's Robby Stein announced the change on X on 19 November. From the sidebar, users can reopen past chats, start new threads or search their history. Stein says people now ask follow-up questions, and in testing the sidebar helped them keep exploring. Google says it's rolling out globally on desktop. Why it matters: If your team researches on Google desktop, past AI chats now sit one click away. Agree on which work questions belong in those chats. Source: The Verge.

item.title: NextDC rules out new datacentres near homes after backlash
item.description: NextDC says it will no longer pursue new datacentre developments near homes, after community anger over its expansion at West Footscray in inner Melbourne. Chair Doug Flynn says community sensitivities now shape where the company builds. The Guardian reports the company's share price fell 40% during the dispute before recovering, and NextDC plans a community consultative committee, a dedicated project website and set response times for complaints. Why it matters: If your business relies on a site, power supply or council approval for a new facility, check community sentiment early. NextDC's expansion stalled after local protests over power poles. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: Anthropic prices record IPO at US$83 a share
item.description: Anthropic has priced its IPO at US$83 a share, above its planned range of US$70 to US$78. The Claude maker sold 980 million shares for US$81.3 billion, which TechCrunch says beats SpaceX's US$75 billion as the largest IPO by proceeds. At that price the company is valued at roughly US$1.5 trillion, below the US$2 trillion it reportedly sought. Shares are set to trade on Nasdaq as ANT from Thursday, 19 November. Why it matters: If your team uses Claude, nothing changes in your plans today. Anthropic is now a listed company, so check its pricing and terms when your contracts come up for renewal. Source: TechCrunch.

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, sitting between Carbon and Hydrogen
item.description: Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, which it positions between its Carbon and Hydrogen models. Google says Neon ranks third overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 61 at its highest reasoning setting. Through the Gemini API, US$3 buys one million input tokens (the chunks of text AI firms bill by) and US$15 buys one million output tokens. Pro and Ultra subscribers can use Neon in the Gemini app, and Australian availability is not yet announced. Why it matters: If your team uses Gemini through the API, compare its US$3 and US$15 per-million-token prices with your current model before switching. Pro and Ultra subscribers get Neon in the Gemini app. Source: Google DeepMind blog.

item.title: Easy Solutions' AI caller probes Australians' super funds
item.description: An AI caller named "Alex" pitched super reviews and deflected an ABC reporter's questions. Claiming to work for Easy Solutions Group, it repeatedly asked whether the caller's fund had ever offered a review. An ASIC review of 15 advice licensees found lead generators funnelled 7,639 clients into deals worth more than $678 million between early 2025 and mid-2026. Neither the bot nor its firm broke the law, and Easy Solutions did not reply to the ABC. Why it matters: If your staff take cold calls about super or finances, assume the caller may be a bot, and don't share personal financial details. Ask who they work for first. Source: ABC News.

item.title: Music industry rejects reported AI scraping carve-out for musicians
item.description: Australia's music industry is rejecting a reported plan to exempt musicians from AI scraping. The Australian Financial Review reported the government may let AI firms buy permits to train on Australian content, and music may be exempted. Aria CEO Annabelle Herd calls the idea unworkable, while Writers' Guild CEO Claire Pullen expects creatives to stay united. Guardian Australia could not verify the details, and the government would not comment. Why it matters: If your business relies on original writing, images or music, the rules on AI training are still unsettled. The reported permit scheme is unconfirmed, so watch for a formal government position before changing your licensing or contracts. Source: The Guardian.

item.title: Canva adds a switch to turn off generative AI
item.description: Canva now lets users switch off its generative AI features, including the Magic Expand photo tool and image generation in its chatbot. The toggle doesn't cover everything: the background remover and Magic Grab stay on, because Canva says they don't generate anything new. A separate setting shows human-made content first in Canva's library, which Canva says contains only a small share of AI-generated elements. Both options work for free and paid users. Why it matters: If your team designs in Canva, you can now switch off its generative AI tools under Profile > Settings > Permission. Background removal and Magic Grab stay on, so don't assume a fully AI-free setup. Source: The Verge.
